Published - October 12, 2026 05:15 am IST - VATICAN CITY

Pope Leo leads the Angelus prayer from the window of the Apostolic Palace at the Vatican, October 11, 2026
                                          | Photo Credit: via Reuters

Pope Leo said on Sunday (October 12, 2026) that ⁠doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery ‌this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff’s tenure.

Leo told pilgrims ‌in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly Sunday ‌prayer ⁠that the growth was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.

“Recently, ⁠during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung,” said the pontiff. “It was detected at a very early stage and ​is well contained.”

“The doctors ‌believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” he said. “The operation is already scheduled for ‌the next few days.”

A nodule on the lung is ​a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than ⁠5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors.

Leo, elected pope by the ‌world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to previously have had health issues.

The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years.

The Vatican press ‌office said Leo’s recovery from surgery was expected to take about ​a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope’s health.

Leo keeps a ⁠busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour of ⁠Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17.

Before mentioning his health issue in his address on ‌Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers “for the pastoral visit I will undertake.”

Pope Leo Announces Upcoming Surgery After Doctors Find Nodule In Lung

‘The doctors believe that it is best to intervene’

Actual Article Body:
(Photo by Ernesto Ruscio/Getty Images)

Pope Leo XIV will undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a small nodule from his lung.

The pope shared the news himself during his Sunday Angelus, telling the faithful gathered for the prayer that recent medical exams had detected the nodule, according to Vatican News.

Doctors caught it early and found the nodule contained within a single area of the lung. They recommended surgery to take it out, and the pope said he would follow their advice. (RELATED: Pope Leo Takes On Assisted Death, Secularism, Education In Blunt Message To French Establishment)

“The doctors believe that it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” Leo said.

Pope Leo: I will undergo surgery soon to remove nodule in my lung https://t.co/QzNwK2Gz7B

The procedure will take place at Rome’s Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic, with the operation set for the first days of this week, according to Vatican News. Holy See press office director Matteo Bruni told reporters the pope should need roughly a week to recover afterward.

The hospital, a Catholic teaching institution, has long served as the site of papal care and keeps a suite reserved for the pope on its 10th floor, according to the Associated Press (AP).

Pope John Paul II had a benign tumor removed from his colon at the same hospital in 1992, the AP reported. Dr. Sergio Alfieri, who leads Gemelli’s digestive surgery department, operated on Pope Francis for a colon ailment in 2021 and repaired a hernia in 2023, according to Catholic News Service. Francis spent several days recovering in the hospital after the hernia repair.

Leo, born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago, became the first U.S.-born pope when cardinals elected him in May 2025 after the death of Pope Francis earlier that year.

The pope closed his address by asking for prayers. “I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers,” he said, according to Vatican News.
